stories.headline: Douglas County man convicted on 18 counts in 'house of terror' assault and child abuse case
stories.summary:
A Douglas County jury on Monday found Dontae Lahmar Burney, 36, guilty on 18 charges tied to a pattern of violence against his girlfriend and several children. The counts include 10 of assault, among them strangulation and assault causing reckless bodily injury; six of child abuse involving bodily injury; and two of menacing. He faces between 10 and 112 years in prison.

Authorities said Burney repeatedly beat and strangled his girlfriend and assaulted several children between March 2023 and June 2024. Evidence at trial included a graphic video showing him beating a 2-year-old for failing to clean his room. Chief Deputy District Attorney Danielle Jaramillo described the home as "a house of terror."

Prosecutors said the verdict sends a message that domestic violence and child abuse will not be tolerated in the 23rd Judicial District. Senior Deputy District Attorney Lauren Raible noted that the most dangerous time for a domestic violence victim is when leaving the relationship. Burney is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. 29.

stories.headline: Two in custody after hours-long standoff in Douglas County following fleeing vehicle
stories.summary:
A man and a woman were taken into custody peacefully Monday after barricading themselves in a car for more than two hours in Douglas County. The Colorado State Patrol first noticed the vehicle near Castle Rock early Monday and tried to stop it after seeing that its plates were stolen and did not match the car.

Troopers backed off when the car sped away, reaching more than 98 mph on I-25. Denver7 asked CSP why it ended the pursuit and had not received a response. Douglas County license plate readers later detected the vehicle on Lincoln Avenue, where deputies stopped it off I-25.

The suspects barricaded themselves so officers could not see inside. Agencies including Parker, Lone Tree, Castle Rock and Littleton police, South Metro Fire Rescue and the regional SWAT team responded. The standoff occurred during the morning rush hour in a heavily traveled area, and the sheriff's office thanked the public for its patience.

stories.headline: Girl critically injured in fiery two-vehicle crash on I-25 near Wyoming border
stories.summary:
A juvenile girl was critically injured Sunday in a two-vehicle crash on northbound Interstate 25 near milepost 298 in Weld County, the Colorado State Patrol said Monday. Troopers found both vehicles fully engulfed in flames shortly before 6 p.m.

According to the preliminary investigation, a 2014 Ford Escape struck the rear of a 2026 Buick Enclave that was stopped and partially blocking the right lane after hitting a deer. Both vehicles caught fire. Firefighters extinguished the flames soon after arriving.

Five people were injured, all from Cheyenne, Wyoming. The girl in the Buick was flown to a hospital in critical condition, and a 29-year-old woman in the Buick and a 23-year-old woman in the Escape had serious injuries. The Buick's driver, 29-year-old Hunter Herzberger, was charged with careless driving causing serious bodily injury. Northbound I-25 was closed for several hours and has reopened.

stories.headline: Denver City Council advances permanent construction relief fund for small businesses
stories.summary:
The Denver City Council on Monday advanced on first reading a proposal to create a permanent program to help small businesses recover from losses caused by major city construction projects. Sponsored by Councilmembers Chris Hinds, Amanda Sawyer and Flor Alvidrez, the Business Impact Opportunity Fund ordinance and a companion ordinance creating a special revenue fund still require final approval.

The program builds on a 2019 pilot created for I-70 construction that has helped more than 3,000 small businesses, but it has no funding for 2027. Projects costing $10 million to $25 million and lasting at least a year could qualify for an allocation of at least 1%, while projects over $25 million lasting 18 months or more could require 1% to 5%.

The money would come from the General Fund, and with the 2027 budget already set, it is unclear how the city would pay for it. Councilmember Kevin Flynn questioned how construction costs would be calculated, and transportation officials said details would be set through administrative rules. Business advocates say eligibility rules have excluded some of the hardest-hit businesses.

stories.headline: Colorado lawmakers weigh Medicaid changes without relying too heavily on Amendment 87
stories.summary:
Colorado's legislative Medicaid Commission approved roughly 60 recommendations this month to retool the state's costly Medicaid program. The proposals cover a range of administrative functions and direct-care services.

Lawmakers also reaffirmed that passage of Amendment 87, the revenue-raising ballot measure, will not spare them from a serious and at times difficult examination of the program.

The recommendations are expected to inform budget deliberations when the legislature convenes in January.

stories.headline: Colorado to try again to ban food assistance spending on soda, Polis says
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis announced that Colorado will once again seek to bar people from using food assistance dollars to buy sweetened drinks. The announcement followed consultation with the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

The move renews an effort to restrict what can be purchased with benefits from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program in the state.

Further details on the timeline and the scope of the restriction were not immediately available.

stories.headline: Denver on pace for one of its latest first snows on record
stories.summary:
Denver has yet to record measurable snow this season, placing it third on the list of latest first snows in records dating to 1882. The National Weather Service lists the latest first snow as Dec. 10, 2021, followed by Nov. 29, 2025, and Nov. 21, 1934.

A first snow counts with just 0.1 inch on the ground. Forecasts show highs in the 50s and 60s and little chance of precipitation through at least Nov. 26, with a second storm Friday through Sunday unlikely to bring snow to the city. Nov. 29 is the date to watch for movement up the rankings, though one Pivotal Weather scenario shows possible accumulation Nov. 28.

Statewide snowpack stands at about 70% of normal for the date, with Southwest Colorado's Wolf Creek Ski Area having received 66 inches. Monday was chilly, with highs in the low to mid 40s, and a 20% chance of snow showers Monday night in Denver. Snow was expected in the mountains, which could affect westbound I-70 evening commutes.

stories.headline: Denver Country Club plans padel courts, ice rink and other upgrades
stories.summary:
Denver Country Club is planning renovations at its 1700 E. 1st Ave. location. The upgrades include padel courts, a new ice rink and pickleball facilities.

The project reflects growing demand for racquet sports at private clubs in the metro area.

Separately, Lunar Outpost is relocating to Arvada and plans to hire 100 employees to build its Pegasus lunar rover for NASA's 2028 moon mission, according to the Denver Business Journal.

stories.headline: Longtime Denver developer Blake Fulenwider joins CBRE in tenant representation
stories.summary:
Blake Fulenwider has joined CBRE's Denver office as a leasing expert, moving to the tenant representation side of commercial real estate. He brings two decades of development experience from his family's company.

The hire marks a switch from developing properties to advising tenants on leasing.

stories.headline: Rockies hire former Mariners manager Scott Servais as senior director of baseball operations
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies have hired former Seattle Mariners manager Scott Servais as senior director of baseball operations, The Athletic reported. Servais spent the past two seasons as a Padres special assistant for player development.

Servais caught for the Rockies in 2000, appearing in 33 games. He managed the Mariners from 2016 to 2024, leading them to the 2022 postseason, their first since 2001. Seattle dismissed him in August 2024.

The hire comes as the Rockies try to rebuild their baseball operations under president Paul DePodesta and general manager Josh Byrnes after a fourth straight 100-loss season. Their 5.59 ERA was the worst in MLB. Separately, catcher Hunter Goodman underwent left shoulder surgery shortly after the season ended, DePodesta confirmed.

stories.headline: Polis volunteers and donates turkeys ahead of Thanksgiving in Colorado Springs and Pueblo
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis was in southern Colorado on Monday, Nov. 23, to volunteer and donate turkeys to families ahead of Thanksgiving. He made stops in Colorado Springs and Pueblo.

Polis encouraged Coloradans to give back to their communities during the holiday season.

The visit comes as the governor nears the end of his term.

topStory.headline: Federal Appeals Court Clears Army to Detonate 9,500 Pounds of Degraded Lead Azide at Iowa Ammunition Plant
topStory.summary:
A federal appeals court ruled Monday that the U.S. Army may proceed with detonating several tons of degraded bomb-making chemicals at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The material consists of 68 barrels containing nearly 9,500 pounds of lead azide, an explosive compound of lead and nitrogen used mainly in detonators and blasting caps. The detonation was initially planned for Friday, but the army has rescheduled it three times amid public concern about possible health and environmental effects.

The ruling, issued by a panel of the Eighth Circuit, followed a day of uncertainty. In a social media post hours earlier, President Donald Trump said he preferred to dispose of the material as soon as possible and that a controlled detonation would be much safer. He said he was making the decision "fully subject to" approval from Iowa's Democratic governor-elect, Rob Sand, and warned that if Sand or the courts did not agree, the government would not proceed and would hold the incoming governor responsible for "any and all death or destruction." Trump also blamed the Obama administration, saying it improperly stored a large number of explosives at the plant in 2009.

Sand, who does not take office until January, called for greater transparency in a statement on social media. He said Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation and why the administration believes the detonation is the best path forward. He noted that he has been receiving briefings from the administration and has asked the federal government to share that information publicly as soon as possible. Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley echoed the call for increased communication with the public but said he supported a controlled, safe removal over a spontaneous catastrophe.

Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, in southeastern Iowa. The army has warned that the blast could release a plume of toxic lead dust extending up to 100 miles to the northeast, potentially reaching communities such as Wapello, Iowa, and New Boston, Illinois. Outgoing Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the state emergency management office Friday, and the state set up a website with information about the detonation. According to the Des Moines Register, a court filing said the lead azide has been vulnerable to temperature swings because the blast doors on the bunkers holding it had been removed.

With the court's ruling in place, the army is free to set a new date for the detonation, though no timetable was confirmed in the available reporting. Officials face continuing pressure to explain the origins of the stockpile, the risks of the operation, and the precautions planned for nearby residents and downwind communities.
